references.text: The immediate context: God drives the human out of the garden to prevent access to the tree of life.
After Adam and Eve were expelled from Eden's garden, the narrative begins about their lives outside, and the birth of Cain and Abel.
The cherubim on the cover of the ark of the covenant reflect the cherubim who guarded the way to the tree of life – both guard God's holy presence.
In the prophecy against the king of Tyre, Eden, God's garden, and the anointed cherub who guards are mentioned – a clear parallel to the cherubim in Gen 3:24.
Moses' exhortation to choose life can be seen in light of the lost access to the tree of life after the fall.
The promise to eat from the tree of life in paradise is given to the one who overcomes – a direct link to the tree of life in Eden's garden.
The tree of life in the new Jerusalem points to the restoration of what was lost when humanity was driven out of Eden's garden.
Those who wash their robes gain the right to the tree of life – the access that was closed off in Gen 3:24 is restored for the saved.

The verses illuminate each other through a dramatic contrast: humanity's original calling to guard the garden together with God, versus God's necessary action to guard the way to the tree of life against humanity after the fall.
